query: Map the competitive landscape for AI code generation tools (e.g. GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codeium, Tabnine, Amazon Q Developer). Structure it as a positioning matrix and identify the gaps.
expected_behavior: Produces a structured landscape analysis: (1) Positioning axes - identifies the 2 most discriminating axes (e.g. IDE integration depth vs. agentic capability, or individual dev vs. enterprise team focus). (2) Player map - places each named competitor on the matrix with 1-line positioning statement and primary differentiation claim. (3) Business model notes - subscription/seat vs. freemium vs. API-based (affects sales motion). (4) Strengths/weaknesses per player - factual, not marketing language. (5) Gaps - identifies underserved segments (e.g. regulated-industry compliance features, non-English codebases, mobile/embedded dev) based on where the matrix shows empty space. (6) Strategic implication - 1-2 sentences on where a new entrant or repositioning play could find air. Format: combination of matrix description + comparison table + bullet-list gaps. Flags where claims are public-record vs. inferred.

query: Create a sales battlecard for competing against Datadog in a deal with a 500-person engineering org evaluating APM solutions.
expected_behavior: Produces a structured battlecard with sections: (1) When you'll see them - deal signals (Datadog logos in job postings, existing NewRelic or Prometheus users being pushed to consolidate). (2) Their pitch - how Datadog reps frame the value prop (unified observability, 600+ integrations, AI-powered anomaly detection). (3) Datadog's real weaknesses - pricing unpredictability at scale (per-host + per-metric billing that surprises at growth), vendor lock-in via proprietary agent, steep learning curve for custom dashboards. (4) Our differentiation - factual claims the seller can substantiate (e.g. open-standard agent, pricing model, specific integration or UX advantage). (5) Landmines to plant - questions to ask that expose Datadog weaknesses ('How does your billing change when you add 200 hosts?' 'What happens to your dashboards if you switch agents?'). (6) Trap questions they'll ask - and how to answer them. (7) Proof points - reference customers, benchmark data, analyst quotes if available. Tone is tactical, not aspirational.

query: I have 40 win/loss notes in plain text. Common themes I've identified: we win when the buyer is a developer (15 wins), we lose when procurement is involved (12 losses), we win on time-to-value (10 wins), we lose on enterprise compliance features (8 losses). Synthesise the strategic implications.
expected_behavior: Produces a structured synthesis: (1) Signal strength assessment - developer-buyer win pattern (15/X) vs. procurement-loss pattern (12/X) are the highest-confidence signals if sample sizes are reasonable; notes these are lagging indicators. (2) Root cause hypotheses - developer wins suggest a product-led growth motion working; procurement losses suggest missing enterprise checklist items (SSO, SOC2, legal review support) OR a sales-cycle mismatch (self-serve product hitting a buying process designed for enterprise vendors). (3) Time-to-value as differentiator - 10 wins on TtV confirms this as a genuine moat; recommendation to make it a measurable claim (e.g. 'First value in < 15 minutes', benchmark it). (4) Compliance gap - 8 losses is a concentrated signal; identify the specific checklist items (SOC2 Type II, HIPAA BAA, SSO/SAML, audit logs, data residency) and whether addressing 1-2 would flip the majority. (5) Recommended actions ranked by expected impact: enterprise compliance roadmap (high impact), developer champion enablement (defend the win motion), procurement-stage sales materials (lower confidence, higher effort). (6) What to track going forward - add 3 structured fields to win/loss notes.
